title.en: A Ship on the Sea and a Book Given to the Old Inca
title.zh: 海上之船與獻給老王的書

region.zh: 庫斯科托科卡奇坊(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The Ynca returned to Cuzco, and he was very old. News came that a ship had been seen on the sea; and after another year a youth entered the city with a great book which he gave to the old Ynca and then disappeared. The Ynca fasted for six months in Tococachi without ceasing.
summary.zh: 印加王返庫斯科,其時已屆暮年。傳來消息:海上有人見一艘船;又過一年,一少年入城,攜一部大書獻與老王,隨即隱去。老王遂在托科卡奇不輟齋戒六個月。

sensitivity.note: The mysterious ship-and-book omen (often read as a premonition of the Spanish arrival); left as Salcamayhua records it.

title.en: Seven Years of Hunger: Amaru Tupac's Farms That Frost Never Touched
title.zh: 七年饑饉:霜所不侵的阿瑪魯·圖帕克之田

region.en: Callachaca and Lucrioc-chullo farms, near Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近卡利亞查卡與盧克里奧克-丘略田莊(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In those days there was a great famine which lasted for seven years, and during that time the seed produced no fruit. Many died of hunger, and it is even said that some ate their own children; the Ynca was then living at Tumipampa. They say that Amaru Tupac Ynca, during those seven years of famine, obtained large harvests from his farms at Callachaca and Lucrioc-chullo: the dews always descended upon them at night, and frost never visited them, insomuch that the people would have worshipped him by reason of the miracle; but Amaru Tupac would not consent to this insult to the Creator. He rather humbled himself, feeding the poor during the seven years of famine, for his disposition was to be humble and meek to all; he had filled the collcas or granaries with food many months before. His descendants were the Ccapac-Ayllu.
summary.zh: 其時大饑七年,播種不實。餓死者眾,相傳竟有人食其子女;其時印加王駐圖米潘帕。相傳七年饑荒中,阿瑪魯·圖帕克·印加在卡利亞查卡與盧克里奧克-丘略的田莊卻大獲豐收:夜夜甘露自降,霜雪從不侵擾。民眾幾欲因此神蹟而拜他為神;但阿瑪魯·圖帕克不肯以此侮辱造物主,反而謙卑自處,七年間賑濟貧民——他天性謙沖,待眾以和;早在數月之前,他的糧倉便已貯滿食糧。其後裔即卡帕克-阿伊柳世系。

sensitivity.note: The refusing-worship motif attached to the prince who declined the throne; a humility exemplum inside the dynastic cycle.

title.en: Chuchi-capac Dressed as a Woman: The Huacas Thrown into Lake Urcos
title.zh: 喬奇-卡帕克扮婦而逃:瓦卡沉入烏爾科斯湖

region.en: Llallahua-pucara and lake of Urcos, Vilcanota (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 利亞利亞瓦-普卡拉與烏爾科斯湖(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: On the death of Pachacuti the provinces of the Puquinas and Collas rebelled from Vilcañota to Chacamarca, making their fortress in Llallahua-pucara with two hundred thousand men. Tupac Ynca Yupanqui allowed the Hanan-Quichuas and Hurin-Quichuas, confident in their prowess, to march against them: twelve thousand marched from Cuzco full of confidence, taking with them a huaca or idol. They began to fight in Huarmi-Pucara with the women of the Quillacas, and the Quichuas were defeated and entirely cut to pieces at the fortress; one man escaped with the news, and Tupac Ynca Yupanqui mourned for the flower of his army. He set out himself with one hundred and twenty thousand men and besieged Llallahua-pucara for three years. Then the Collas offered up sacrifices to the sun, of children and cuis, and from the air there was an encouraging answer to their Tayta; then they waged war without any fear. But the Ynca attacked with renewed fury; at sunrise on the third day he drove back the Collas. Chuchi-Ccapac and his chiefs escaped to the province of the Lupacas dressed as women. They were brought before the Ynca in the town of Cac-yaviri with the huaca of Ynti and other huacas; Tupac Ynca Yupanqui ordered the chiefs and the huacas to be placed in the centre of their army of one hundred thousand men, where they were insulted - he sent for the huyachucos, suyuntus, llama-llamas and chuñires to trample upon them - and eventually they were thrown into the lake of Urcos, while the Collas were brought in triumph to Cuzco. In memory of these cruel wars the Ynca ordered two darts of gold and silver to be placed in Vilcañota.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提一死,普基納與科利亞諸省自維爾卡尼奧塔至查卡馬爾卡叛亂,以二十萬之眾據利亞利亞瓦-普卡拉為堡。圖帕克·尤潘琪拗不過自信滿滿的哈南與烏林基丘亞人,許其出征:一萬二千人攜一尊瓦卡自庫斯科昂然而行。他們在瓦爾米-普卡拉與基利亞卡之婦交戰,大敗;退至主堡又被科利亞人圍殲殆盡,僅一人逃歸報信。圖帕克·尤潘琪哀其精銳盡喪,親率十二萬人圍堡三年。科利亞人向太陽獻孩童與豚鼠為祭,空中竟有聲音鼓舞其祭司「塔伊塔」;他們遂無所畏懼而戰。然而印加王攻勢愈猛,第三日日出時大破科利亞軍。喬奇-卡帕克與諸酋扮作婦女逃往盧帕卡省,在卡克-亞維里鎮被押至印加王前,連同「因蒂」瓦卡及諸瓦卡。王命將酋長與瓦卡置於十萬大軍正中受辱——召來惠亞丘科、蘇雲圖斯、利亞馬-利亞馬斯、丘尼雷斯踏踐之——最後盡投烏爾科斯湖中,科利亞人則被凱旋押解庫斯科。為誌此慘烈戰事,印加王在維爾卡尼奧塔立金銀標槍各一。

sensitivity.note: Colla defeat cycle; the sun-oracle that answered the besieged is a notable case of an oracle answering the losing side.

passages.text: On his death the provinces of the Puquinas and Collas rebelled, from Vilcañota to Chacamarca, with all the Urco-suyus of Achacache, Huancane, Asillu, and Asancaru, and they made their fortress in Llallahua-pucara with two hundred thousand men. So Tupac Ynca Yupanqui assembled an army to attack them; and the Hanan-Quichuas and Hurin-Quichuas, confident in their prowess, petitioned to be allowed to march against the enemy. At last the Ynca yielded to their importunity, and a very powerful army of twelve thousand Quichuas marched from Cuzco, full of confidence, well armed, taking with them a huaca, or idol. They began to fight in Huarmi-Pucara with the women of the Quillacas, and the Quichuas were defeated. They retired to the principal fortress of Llallahua-pucara, where they were besieged by the Collas and entirely cut to pieces. One man escaped, and brought the news to Tupac Ynca Yupanqui, who mourned for the flower of his army.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he set out himself from Cuzco with one hundred and twenty thousand men, and marched against the Collas, laying siege to the said fortress of Llallahua-pucara. This siege lasted for three years. Then the Collas offered up sacrifices to the sun, of children and cuis, and from the air there was an encouraging answer to their Tayta (Tayta means a minister of the huacas). Then they waged war upon the Ynca without any fear; but it fell out very differently from what they expected, for the Ynca attacked these Collas with renewed fury, and there was much bloodshed. On the third day the Ynca and his captains renewed the assault at sunrise and drove back the Collas.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Chuchi-Ccapac and his chiefs escaped to the province of the Lupacas dressed as women. They were brought before the Ynca in the town of Cac-yaviri, with the huaca of Ynti and other huacas. Tupac Ynca Yupanqui ordered the chiefs and the huacas to be placed in the centre of their army of one hundred thousand men, where they were insulted, and, to increase the affront, he sent for the huyachucos, suyuntus, llama-llamas, and chuñires to trample upon them, and eventually they were thrown into the lake of Urcos, while the Collas were brought in triumph to Cuzco. In memory of these cruel wars of the Collas, the Ynca ordered two darts of gold and silver to be placed in Vilcañota, and he left mitimaes and garrisons of loyal men for the security of the conquered provinces.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Huarmi-auca: The Province of Women Across the Great River
title.zh: 瓦爾米-奧卡:大河彼岸的女兒國

region.en: Huarmi-auca, eastern forests beyond the great river (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 大河以東森林中的女兒國(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The Ynca assembled 200,000 men to undertake a new conquest in the Andes, naming Uturuncu Achachi as general. These did good service in the conquest of the provinces of Manaresu and Upatari, as far as the confines of Huancavillca on one side and to Caravaya on the other, where they met with a province inhabited entirely by women, called Huarmi-auca. They then crossed a river of great volume; but at first, as no man could pass over, some audacious monkeys, belonging to a chief of the Manares, went across, and secured ropes and cables after overcoming great difficulties. This province is called the Golden, and in it they found a great and rich land called Escay-oya, with a very warlike race of people who were said to be cannibals; and they make such deadly poison, that it would seem they have a pact with the devil. They fought two desperate battles, and in the third they were defeated by the soldiers of the Ynca - not because they were less brave, but by superiority of arms and discipline. News then came that Tupac Ynca Yupanqui had banished a captain to a province of the Chirihuanas; Apu Quillacta proclaimed the news to his people, and they returned to their own land, leaving the Ynca army with the general - and Uturuncu Achachi returned to Cuzco, abandoning the conquests made by the labours of three armies.
summary.zh: 印加王集兵二十萬征安第斯之東,以烏圖倫庫·阿查奇為將。軍鋒經馬納雷蘇、烏帕塔里,東抵萬卡維利卡界,西至卡拉瓦亞,途中遇一省,居民全為女子,名「瓦爾米-奧卡」(女戰之地)。繼而欲渡一條極寬的大河;起初無人能渡,馬納雷斯酋長豢養的幾隻大膽猴子竟泅水而過,歷盡艱險,為大軍取回繩索纜索。此省名「金省」,其中有沃土名「埃斯卡伊-奧亞」,其民驍勇,相傳食人,又製劇毒,彷彿與魔鬼有約。兩場惡戰不分勝負,第三戰方為印加軍所敗——非其不勇,實因兵器與紀律之優。此時傳來圖帕克·尤潘琪放逐一將至奇里瓜納之地的消息;阿普·基利亞克塔向部眾宣告,眾人便棄軍歸鄉。烏圖倫庫·阿查奇只得班師回庫斯科,三軍將士浴血所拓之土,盡皆棄之。

sensitivity.note: Amazonian frontier legend inside an Inca chronicle; the land-of-women topos is compared across traditions.

passages.text: The Ynca then assembled 200,000 men to undertake a new conquest in the Andes, naming Uturuncu Achachi as general of the army. These did good service in the conquest of the provinces of Manaresu and Upatari, as far as the confines of Huancavillca on one side, and to Caravaya on the other, where they met with a province inhabited entirely by women, called Huarmi-auca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: They then crossed a river of great volume; but at first, as no man could pass over, some audacious monkeys, belonging to a chief of the Manares, went across, and secured ropes and cables after overcoming great difficulties. This province is called the Golden, and in it they found a great and rich land called Escay-oya, with a very warlike race of people who were said to be cannibals; and they make such deadly poison, that it would seem they have a pact with the devil. They fought two desperate battles, and in the third they were defeated by the soldiers of the Ynca, not because they were less brave, but by superiority of arms and discipline.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: They say that while these new provinces were being numbered, news came that Tupac Ynca Yupanqui had banished a captain to a province of the Chirihuanas. The captain, Apu Quillacta, proclaimed this news to his people, and they returned to their own land, leaving the Ynca army with the general, Uturuncu Achachi. This was the reason that the Escay-oyas, and Upataxis, and Manares again took up arms, for the forces of Uturuncu Achachi were reduced; and he returned to Cuzco, abandoning the conquests made by the labours of three armies and at great cost of lives.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Three Hundred Porters Buried with Their Gold at Pachatusan
title.zh: 三百腳夫與黃金同葬帕查圖桑

region.en: Hill of Pachatusan, above Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科上方帕查圖桑山(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: At this time there came from the Andes of Upatari three hundred Antis laden with gold in dust and tubes, and at the moment of their arrival it began to freeze, and all the crops were frozen to the roots. So, by advice of the old councillors, the Ynca ordered the three hundred men to carry their loads of gold to Pachatusun, a very high hill, and there to have them buried. So the unfortunates were killed and buried as a welcome.
summary.zh: 其時,自烏帕塔里安第斯來了三百名安蒂人,背負金沙與金管。他們抵達之際,天氣驟然結凍,莊稼連根凍斃。於是,依老臣之議,印加王命這三百人將黃金背負至極高的帕查圖桑山,就地埋藏。可憐的三百人遂被處死,與金同葬——作為對山神的「迎禮」。

sensitivity.note: A killing recorded with terrible economy ('as a welcome'); grouped with the Capacocha-like mountain offerings.

passages.text: At this time there came from the Andes of Upatari three hundred Antis laden with gold in dust and tubes, and at the moment of their arrival it began to freeze, and all the crops were frozen to the roots. So, by advice of the old councillors, the Ynca ordered the three hundred men to carry their loads of gold to Pachatusun, a very high hill, and there to have them buried. So the unfortunates were killed and buried as a welcome.

title.en: The Governor's Plot and the Uncle's Dream: Saving the Child Huayna Capac
title.zh: 攝政之謀與叔父之夢:救下幼主瓦伊納·卡帕克

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The Ynca died, being very old, as well as his brother Amaru Tupac Ynca: both died in the same year, leaving Huayna Ccapac Ynca as their heir, and Apu Hualpaya as governor, for the heir was of tender age. They buried many yanacunas, pachacas, women and servants beloved by the Ynca, whom the barbarous captains thought their Ynca would require to be served in the next world. This governor intended to raise himself to be ruler of Ttahuantin-suyu, ordering troops to be secretly assembled from all parts for a given day; he began to worship the sun and moon and thunder, assigning estates for these false gods, and some evil-disposed Curacas executed his orders with alacrity. One night a bastard uncle of Huayna Ccapac was lying half awake and half asleep, very early in the morning, when he saw troops headed by Hualpaya surrounding the city, and pointing their arrows at the child Huayna Ccapac. This was a dream; but the uncle jumped up as if it had been true, and went to the house of Cuys Manco.
summary.zh: 印加王年邁而終,其弟阿瑪魯·圖帕克·印加亦於同年去世;幼主瓦伊納·卡帕克年齒尚幼,由阿普·瓦爾帕亞攝政。眾人埋葬了先王生前鍾愛的雅納庫納、帕查卡斯、婦女與僕從——野蠻的將領們以為先王在來世仍需這些人侍奉。攝政王則欲自立為大蘇尤之主,密令各處調兵,定期舉事;他開始崇拜太陽、月亮與雷,為這些「偽神」撥賜田產,一些懷有異心的庫拉卡聞命而動。一夜拂曉,瓦伊納·卡帕克的庶叔半睡半醒之際,夢見瓦爾帕亞率兵圍城,箭簇盡指幼主瓦伊納·卡帕克。此雖一夢,叔父卻霍然而起,如夢成真一般,逕往庫伊斯·曼科家中而去。

sensitivity.note: Dream-warning episode; the human retinue burials are recorded as given.

passages.text: The Ynca died, being very old, as well as his brother Amaru Tupac Ynca, who had attained a great age. Both the brothers died in the same year, leaving Huayna Ccapac Ynca as their heir, and Apu Hualpaya as governor, for the heir was of tender age. They mourned for the Ynca as they had done for Pachacuti, forming two armies, one of men and the other of women, and they buried many yanacunas, pachacas, women, and servants, who were beloved by the Ynca. The barbarous captains thought that their Ynca would require to be served in the next world by these people.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: They say that this governor and coadjutor intended to raise himself to be ruler of Ttahuantin-suyu, and that he ordered troops to be secretly assembled from all parts for a given day. They say that this governor began to worship the sun and moon and thunder; and Huayna Ccapac, being a young child, also adored them. And they say that the governor assigned estates for these false gods, and that some evil disposed Curacas executed his orders with alacrity.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: This Hualpaya was now ready to rebel without the knowledge of the provinces; and one night a bastard uncle of Huayna Ccapac was lying half awake and half asleep, very early in the morning, when he saw troops headed by Hualpaya surrounding the city, and pointing their arrows at the child Huayna Ccapac. This was a dream; but the uncle jumped up as if it had been true, went to the house of Cuys Manco, and gave the alarm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)
